info.name: Loopd'n API v4
info.description:
# Loopd'n API v4

Every reply is wrapped in the same envelope:

```json
{ "code": 1, "message": "...", "data": { } }
```

`code` is `1` for success and `-1` for failure; the HTTP status stays meaningful. `data` is the payload, or the field errors on a failure.

## Start here
1. **Register**, then **Verify email** (the code is in the server log when `DEBUG` is on).
2. **Login** - stores your tokens automatically.
3. **Request phone code** then **Verify phone** - without a verified number your account can never receive a group text.
4. **Create group** - stores `conversation_id` and gives the group its own phone number.

## What is new since v3
- **`12. WhatsApp`** - optional: a group owner connects their own WhatsApp Business number through Meta's Embedded Signup (from profile settings, or when inviting by WhatsApp), attaches it to their groups, and invites members, who opt in with START. Messages then flow both ways over that number. `Cleanup` is now folder 13.
- **`11. Calls & recordings`** - voice and video calls in any conversation you belong to, on LiveKit. Django authorises the call, enforces the plan's participant limit and hands the browser a short-lived token; LiveKit carries the media, so **audio and video never pass through this API**. Recording (to S3), its retention and its permissions are here too. *Plan* objects gained `max_call_participants`, `has_screen_share`, `has_call_recording` and `call_recording_retention_days`.
- **Call events arrive on the existing websocket**, `/ws/chat/`, to everyone in the conversation: `call.incoming`, `call.accepted`, `call.rejected`, `call.ended`, `call.recording.started` and `call.recording.stopped`. Each carries `call_id`, `conversation_id`, `user_id` (who caused it) and the whole `call`. `call.incoming` is not sent to the person who started the call. There is no second socket, and no token ever travels on one.
- **`10. Enterprise`** - the Plan Builder's own catalog-driven flow: a public pricing catalog, drafts (anonymous-allowed, attachable to an account on login), checkout into a frozen `EnterpriseContract` with a line-itemized Stripe invoice, billing status, and the message-credit ledger. Shares the Billing folder's Stripe webhook endpoint rather than adding a second one.
- **`9. Web push`** - the VAPID public key, registering/forgetting a browser subscription so it can be notified while the app is closed.
- **`8. Billing`** - the four platform plans (Free, Premium, Business, Enterprise), Pay-As-You-Go Communication Credit packages, a billing summary, Stripe Checkout for both a plan subscription and a credit top-up, the Stripe billing portal, and the Stripe webhook that keeps `Subscription` and the wallet in sync.
- **Plan limits are enforced.** *Create group* and *Add members* now return `403` once a Free/Premium/Business plan's `max_groups` or `max_members_per_group` would be exceeded - see *List plans*.

## What was new in v3
- **Every URL now ends in a slash.** v1 and v2 stripped it, and Django answers a slash-less POST with a 301 that drops the body - so every write request in them silently did nothing.
- **Payloads fixed**: `Register` and `Reset password` were missing `confirm_password`; `Google sign-in` sent `id_token` where the serializer wants `credential`; `Update my profile` sent an `sms_enabled` that no serializer declares.
- **Runs top to bottom.** Verify email now precedes Login, the join code is fetched before it is used, and *Delete a group* moved to its own final folder instead of destroying the group halfway through.
- **Forgot / reset / change password** were missing entirely.
- **`GET .../participants/`** - the member list, paginated ten at a time. Conversation payloads no longer embed it.

## What was new in v2
- **Every group has its own phone number.** Bought on creation in the creator's country, never changes, deleted with the group.
- **Membership has states** - active, pending, left, removed, blocked - and four join modes.
- **Roles**: promote and demote admins.
- **Broadcast groups** where only admins post.
- **Members without accounts**, reachable only by SMS.
- **Delivery settings** per group, and account-wide.
- **The inbound SMS webhook.**

## Two things that surprise people
**404 means "not yours".** Access control is the database query, not a check bolted on top - so a conversation you are not in is indistinguishable from one that does not exist. That is deliberate.

**Two SMS switches.** `MessagingSettings.sms_enabled` (account-wide) and `Participant.sms_enabled` (this group). Both must be on, plus a verified number, plus consent for members with no account.

request.description:
Create an account.

`phone_number` is **optional but load-bearing for SMS**: a group texts its members on the number they verified, so an account without one can take part in the app and can never be reached by text.

Returns `201` with the account and a `verification` block. A delivery failure still returns `201` with `verification: null` - the account is already committed at that point, and failing the request would strand the user with an account they cannot use.

Confirm the emailed code and receive tokens.

This sets `Profile.email_verified`, **not** `user.is_active`. The two are kept apart on purpose: `is_active` means "an admin has not banned this account", and a verification code must never be able to write it - otherwise a banned user could change their email and verify their way back in.

**Register and verify your email first** - with email verification on, this returns 401 until the account is verified, and *Verify email* already hands back a token pair of its own.

The test script stores the token pair and `user_id`, which everything else authenticates with.

`username` accepts a username **or** an email address.

`401` is deliberately identical for "no such user" and "wrong password", so this cannot be used to discover which accounts exist.
Send a new email verification code. Rate limited per address and per account.

Sign in with a Google ID token, creating the account on first use.

A Google account arrives with a verified email and **no phone number**, so it cannot receive group texts until one is added and verified under *Phone verification*.
Exchange a refresh token for a new access token.

Email a password-reset link.

Always answers the same way whether or not the address exists - a different reply for an unknown address would turn this into a way to discover who has an account.

Finish the reset with the `uid` and `token` out of the emailed link.

Both are single-use: the token stops working once the password changes, so a leaked link cannot be replayed.
Change your own password while signed in. `old_password` is required - an access token alone must not be enough to lock the real owner out.
Blacklist the refresh token. The access token stays valid until it expires.
Username, email and verification state.
Changing the email address clears `email_verified` and sends a new code - otherwise anybody could move a verified badge onto an address they do not own.

Display name, avatar, phone number, whether the number and email are verified, and `email_enabled`.

**`sms_enabled` is not in this payload.** "Send and receive Loop messages by text" lives on *Get my settings*, under `messaging`.

Setting `phone_number` here clears `phone_no_verified` - a number is only trusted once proved, and an unverified number is never texted. Send `avatar` as form-data to set a photo.

**The two SMS switches, and why neither is set here:**

| Switch | Set by | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MessagingSettings.sms_enabled` | *Update a settings screen* (`messaging`) | "Send and receive Loop messages by text": **every** group, both ways. |
| `Participant.sms_enabled` | *Delivery settings*, or **texting STOP / START** to that group's number | whether **one group** texts you - and, after STOP, takes your texts. |

Both must be on for a text to go out.

`sms_enabled` is **not a field on this endpoint**, and sending it here does nothing: DRF drops keys a serializer does not declare, so the request returns 200 and the switch is unchanged.
Every settings screen at once, keyed by name: `appearance`, `messaging`, `notifications`, `privacy`, `security`. Always your own - there is no id in the URL.
One screen. Swap `privacy` for any of the five names; anything else is 404.

Send only the fields you are changing; the answer is the whole screen. An unknown choice is 400 with the field named. PUT is 405.

**Shown but never written here** - if sent they are ignored and the request still returns 200:

- `security.two_factor_enabled` / `two_factor_method` - turning two-factor on must prove the phone or email first, and that flow does not exist yet.

`messaging.sms_enabled` is "Send and receive Loop messages by text" for every group, both ways; a STOP to one group's number is separate and lives on that membership. `messaging.email_enabled` is the same switch as `email_enabled` on *Update my profile*.

Find somebody by username prefix, or by **exact** phone number.

Phone matching is exact and requires the number to be **verified**. A prefix search would let anyone walk the directory a digit at a time, and an unverified match would hand back whoever merely typed someone else's number into their profile.
Public view of another account. Never includes email or phone number.

Text a verification code.

**This is what makes SMS work for you.** A group texts its members on the number they verified here; until this is done your account is app-only.

Omit `phone_number` to re-send to the one already on the profile. Rate limited per account **and** per destination number - one account working through many numbers and many accounts hammering one number are different attacks, and counting only one misses the other.
Confirm the code. Sets `phone_no_verified`, which is what every SMS path checks before texting you.

Every conversation you are an **active** member of, newest activity first.

Access control is the queryset itself: a conversation you are not in does not appear here and 404s everywhere else, so you cannot learn it exists. Members who left, were removed or are still pending are excluded.

Create a group. You become its admin.

**The group is given its own phone number**, in the country of whoever created it, read from their verified number. That number never changes, and it is deleted when the group is.

The number comes back as `sms_number`, an object of `number`, `country`, `status` and `provider`. The whole object may be `null` for a moment: buying it is a call to the telecom provider, made after the group is committed, so a slow provider cannot turn "create a group" into "create nothing".

An **empty `provider`** means no provider is configured and the number is a placeholder - well-formed, but it belongs to nobody and texting it does nothing. Do not tell a user to text a number whose `provider` is empty.

`members` takes usernames or **verified** `+E.164` numbers. Send an image by switching this request to form-data.

**Plan limits apply.** Creating a group beyond your plan's `max_groups` (see *9. Billing*) returns `403`.

One conversation: its settings, its latest message, its `sms_number`, and who runs it.

| Field | |
| --- | --- |
| `created_by` | who started it, as `{username, avatar}` |
| `is_admin` | whether **you** administer it - the creator counts automatically, anyone else needs the admin role |
| `admin_details` | who administers it, as `{username, avatar}`. A group can have several admins and this is one object, so it prefers the creator, then the earliest to join |

`is_admin` and `admin_details` are group concepts: a one-to-one gets `false` and `null`.

**No `participants`.** The member list is unbounded and every row nests a user and a profile, so a group of two hundred would put two hundred profiles in every fetch - and once per conversation on the list endpoint. Use *List members* instead.

`sms_number` is read-only everywhere and for everybody. It is saved in members' phones as the group's name, so a number that could be reassigned would deliver a stranger's messages.

Fields: `number`, `country`, `status`, `provider`. An empty `provider` marks a placeholder that cannot actually receive text.

Admins only. Every field optional.

The seven settings go **inside `settings`**, the same object `POST /group/` takes - there is one shape to learn. Sending them at the top level is silently ignored: DRF drops fields a serializer does not declare, so the request returns 200 and changes nothing.

All seven come back under `settings` on the conversation object, the same shape you sent - so a settings screen renders from one fetch and there is one shape to learn. `join_code` does not: it has its own admin-only endpoint.

**`join_mode`** - how somebody who is not a member gets in:

| Value | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `open` | anyone with the number or link joins immediately |
| `code` | they must supply the group code |
| `approval` | they ask; an admin approves or declines |
| `invite` | nobody can ask; an admin adds them |

New groups default to `invite`, the only mode that cannot surprise anybody. Switching to `code` generates a code if the group has none.

**`mode`** - `chat` (everybody posts) or `broadcast` (only admins post; members still read). Enforced on every route at once, including inbound SMS.

Editing settings deliberately does **not** bump the group up everyone's conversation list. Only a message is activity.

The reply is the conversation - which carries no `participants` on any endpoint. Use *List members* for the member list.

Open the one-to-one conversation with somebody, creating it only once. Safe to call every time a name is tapped: the same pair always resolves to the same conversation.

`identifier` is a username or a **verified** `+E.164` number. Direct conversations have no phone number - SMS is a group feature.

Who is in this conversation, **ten at a time**.

Its own endpoint rather than a field on every conversation reply: the member list is unbounded and each row carries a nested user and profile, so a group of two hundred made every fetch of the group carry two hundred profiles.

Returns the standard page envelope inside `data`:

```
{ "count": 17, "next": "...?page=2", "previous": null,
  "results": [ ...participants... ] }
```

`page_size` raises the page up to a maximum of 100. **Active members only** - somebody who left, was removed or is waiting on approval is not a member; pending requests have their own endpoint, *Join requests*.

A non-member gets **404**, not 403 - access control here is the queryset, so an outsider cannot learn the conversation exists.

Usernames or **verified** numbers of existing accounts.

**Admins only by default, but not always.** The gate is `may_add_members`, so in a group whose `add_member_permission` is `members`, any active member may add people.

All or nothing: if one identifier cannot be resolved, or one person is blocked, nobody is added. To add somebody who has **no account**, use *Invite by phone* instead.

**Plan limits apply.** Adding people past the group owner's plan `max_members_per_group` (see *9. Billing*) returns `403`.

Add somebody who has **no LoopD account**, by their number. Admins only. This is the way into an `invite` group.

A name is required - they never chose one, and without it the group would see a masked number.

**They are texted an invitation and receive nothing from the group until they reply `YES`.** Somebody else putting your number into a group is not you agreeing to be texted. The exact wording sent is stored on the row, because that is what a consent complaint turns on.

**Admins only.** Deliberately not on the conversation payload: the code is what lets a stranger in, so handing it to every member on every fetch would spread it through logs, caches and screenshots far beyond the people who administer the group.

`POST` to the same URL issues a new code, which is how a leaked one is revoked.
Issue a new code. The old one stops working immediately.

Join a group using the code from its shareable link.

Always by code, never by id - otherwise this endpoint would be a way to walk group ids and join every open group in the product.

An unknown code, an invite-only group and a group you are blocked from all return the **same** refusal, byte for byte. Any difference would confirm that a guessed code is real.

On an `approval` group the response is `{"status": "pending"}` and no conversation - you are not a member yet.

Admins only. Everybody waiting to be let into an `approval` group.

Admins are also pushed a `conversation.request` event over the websocket as requests arrive, so the queue does not have to be polled.

Admins only. `decision` is `approve` or `decline`.

Somebody with no account is **texted** either way, because they have no other way of finding out. Somebody with an account is not - they see it in the app, and texting them is a charge for something they already know.

Approval re-checks identity across both a phone number and an account: a pending request can be the same person as a row blocked under their other identifier, and the queue does not show that.

Give a member with **no account** a name. Admins only.

Somebody who joined by texting `JOIN` never gave one, so the group sees a masked number until an admin puts a name to it. A member who has an account keeps their own name - otherwise an admin could relabel another person in the group.

Admins only. `block: true` also stops them rejoining by **any** route - the join code, an admin re-adding them, texting `JOIN`, or registering an account on a blocked number.

An admin cannot remove themselves (use *Leave*), and the last admin cannot be removed at all.

**A block currently cannot be undone through the API.**

Take yourself out of a group. Your messages stay.

Refused for the last admin - hand over with *Change a role* first. Refused on a one-to-one conversation, because there is no way back into one.

Promote a member to admin, or demote them. Admins only.

**This is also how a group's only admin gets out.** Leaving and being removed both refuse to take the last admin, because a group with none has no route back to having one - so hand over first, then leave.

Somebody with no account cannot be an admin: every admin action is an authenticated request, so the role would be unusable while still counting towards that guard.

How **this** conversation reaches **you**. Both fields optional; only what you send is written.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `muted` | silence this group on every channel. What texting `MUTE` sets. |
| `sms_enabled` | whether texts are one of this group's channels for you. Off means app-only. |

`sms_enabled` defaults **on** and `muted` defaults **off** - you verified a number so your groups could reach you on it. These are yours alone; an admin cannot set them for somebody else.

Newest first, paginated.

**`?after_id=<id>` resumes.** Returns only messages newer than that id, **oldest first**, so a client that reconnects can fetch exactly what it missed and append it in order. Without it a client can only re-page the newest-first history and diff, which is unbounded and gets worse the longer it was disconnected.

Keyed on `id` rather than `created_at` deliberately: created_at is app-server wall clock, so two tasks can stamp messages out of order, and it has no tiebreak. Ids come from one sequence.

Each message carries a `source`: `app`, `sms` or `system`. There is **one message per message** however it arrived - a text sent from a handset and one typed in the app are the same row.

A message sent by somebody with no account has `sender.id` and `sender.username` null, and their name in `sender.profile.display_label`. Render that field and both kinds work without branching.

**`client_id` makes a retry safe.** It is your own id for this message. A send that times out - or a websocket that drops mid-send - leaves you unable to tell whether it landed; retrying with the SAME `client_id` returns the message already stored instead of posting a second one. Without it, a retry creates a second row with a different id that no client-side dedupe can collapse, and schedules a **second billed SMS fan-out to every member's phone**.

Optional, scoped per conversation, and echoed back on the message so you can match it to the entry you rendered optimistically. `{{$guid}}` is a Postman variable that generates a fresh one per send.

Post to the conversation. Text, attachments, or both - but not neither.

The message goes to app members over the websocket immediately, and is **fanned out by SMS** to every member who should receive it - excluding you. Who that is depends on their delivery settings, their consent, and whether their number is verified; every decision not to send is recorded with a reason.

In a `broadcast` group a non-admin gets `403`.

**`mentions` are PARTICIPANT ids, not names.** Most members have no handle to parse - they are a number with a display name, and two of them can be called "Mum" - so the composer sends the ids it offered and the words stay plain, which is what makes the SMS and email copies read as written. An id that is not an ACTIVE member of THIS conversation is dropped silently rather than refusing the message. `mention_everyone` is the `@everyone` flag, usable by any member.

Somebody who is mentioned, or whose message is replied to, is notified even when they have turned group messages off - unless they muted the group, which silences everything.

Multipart. Repeat `attachments` for several files.

SMS members cannot receive a photo, so they get a line telling them to open the app rather than an empty message.

**Called by the telecom provider, not by a client.** Included so the inbound path can be exercised without a real phone.

Authenticated by an Ed25519 signature over the raw body, not by a token. With `TELNYX_PUBLIC_KEYS` unset (development) the signature is not checked and this request works as written.

### Status codes are the contract
A provider reads any non-2xx as "resend this", so:

| Code | When |
| --- | --- |
| `200` | anything we understand and will not change our mind about - duplicate, unknown number, unknown sender, malformed |
| `403` | bad signature - DRF answers 403, not 401, because the authentication class returns no WWW-Authenticate header |
| `500` | we failed to handle it - **please do resend** |

### Commands
`JOIN [code]`, `HELP`, `MUTE`, `UNMUTE`, `LEAVE`, `STOP`, `YES`. A command must be the **whole message** - "stop by the shop" is a message to your family, not an opt-out.

Repeat with the same `data.id` to see de-duplication: the second call returns `duplicate: true` and posts nothing.

The pricing page: Free, Premium, Business, Enterprise - their monthly price, group/member/admin limits, storage, call limits (`max_call_participants`, `has_screen_share`, `has_call_recording`, `call_recording_retention_days` - `null` means unlimited / kept until deleted), and whether WhatsApp/Telegram are included.

Public, so a logged-out visitor sees pricing before signing up. `price_display` is `"Custom"` for Enterprise, which is quoted by sales rather than charged through Stripe - `monthly_price_cents` is `null` for the same reason.

The Pay-As-You-Go Communication Credit top-ups: Starter ($5) through High Volume ($100). `credit_cents` is what lands in the wallet - today it matches `price_cents` exactly, but the two are separate fields so a future bonus package (pay $10, get $12 of credit) is just a row where they differ.

Public, for the same reason *List plans* is.

What the caller is on right now: their `subscription` (plan, status, renewal date), their `wallet` (balance, auto-recharge), and - if they have one - `enterprise_credits`.

Every user has both a subscription and a wallet from the moment they sign up - a fresh account is on the Free plan with a zero-balance wallet, not a missing row, so a client never has to special-case "no subscription yet".

`enterprise_credits` is `null` unless the caller has an active or past-due Enterprise contract (see `9. Enterprise`); when present it carries `contract_number`, `status`, `balance` and `monthly_allowance`, all counted in messages, not cents - a separate figure from `wallet.balance_cents`, which is the pay-as-you-go SMS wallet. Once checkout completes, `subscription.plan` also switches from Free to a Plan mirroring the contract's own limits and features, so this one response is enough to show what the caller's account can do without a second, Enterprise-specific call.

Analytics access is feature-gated by the caller's current plan.

If the plan has **Basic Analytics** (or **Advanced Analytics**), the response includes the `basic` section: conversation counts and 30-day message activity.

If the plan has **Advanced Analytics**, `advanced` is included with group-admin and group-size signals. Otherwise `advanced` is `null`.

The endpoint also returns `suggestions`, tailored by access level (`none`, `basic`, `advanced`) so clients can guide upgrades or improvements.

What the caller has paid, newest first: plan subscription payments (the first invoice and every renewal), custom Enterprise plan payments, and credit top-ups. Wallet usage is not here - this lists money paid, not credits spent.

`range` is `7d`, `15d`, `30d` or `custom`, and defaults to `30d` when left out. The presets count back from now. For `custom`, see *Transaction history: custom range*.

Add `kind=plan_subscription`, `kind=enterprise_plan` or `kind=credit_purchase` to narrow the list to one kind of payment.

Paged: `data` carries `count`, `next`, `previous` and `results`. `page_size` defaults to 20 and is capped at 100.

Each result has `id`, `kind`, `kind_label`, `amount_cents`, `currency`, `description`, `stripe_reference`, `receipt_url` and `paid_at`. `amount_cents` is what Stripe charged - for a top-up, the package's price, not the credit it bought. `receipt_url` is Stripe's hosted invoice or receipt page and can be an empty string.

Payments are recorded as Stripe reports them, so an account that paid before this endpoint existed shows nothing older until `python manage.py backfill_billing_payments` has been run.

The same list as *Transaction history*, between two dates of the caller's choosing.

`start_date` and `end_date` are `YYYY-MM-DD` and both are required when `range=custom`. Both days are included in full, in the server's timezone.

**400** if either date is missing, is not a date, or `end_date` is before `start_date` - `data` names the field at fault. An unknown `range` is a 400 too.

Start a Stripe Checkout Session that subscribes the caller to Premium or Business on completion. Redirect the browser/webview to the returned `checkout_url`; Stripe redirects back to `success_url` or `cancel_url` when the customer is done.

Free needs no checkout, and Enterprise is quoted by sales - both return `400` here. A plan whose Stripe price has not been synced yet (`manage.py sync_stripe_billing`) also returns `400`.

The actual upgrade happens off the `checkout.session.completed` webhook, not this response - the session can be abandoned, so nothing changes until Stripe confirms it was paid.

Start a Stripe Checkout Session (one-time payment, not a subscription) that tops up the caller's Communication Wallet on completion. Same redirect shape as *Checkout: subscribe to a plan*.

The wallet is credited off the webhook once Stripe confirms payment, with a ledger row recorded against it - see *Billing summary* for the resulting balance.

A link to Stripe's own hosted page for updating a card, viewing invoices, or cancelling a subscription. Redirect to `portal_url`; Stripe sends the customer back to `return_url` when they are done.

Nothing here is stored locally - Stripe is the source of truth for payment methods, and the webhook is what brings a cancellation back into `Subscription.status`.

**Called by Stripe, not by a client.** Included so the shape of the account-facing events this project understands is documented in one place: `checkout.session.completed` (subscription activation or a credit top-up), `customer.subscription.updated`, `customer.subscription.deleted`, `invoice.paid`, `invoice.payment_failed` and `charge.refunded`. The catalog-sync events (`product.*`, `price.*`) are a separate example below.

Authenticated by a signature over the raw body (`Stripe-Signature` header, verified against `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET`), not a token - like the SMS webhook, this endpoint has no other way to prove Stripe sent it. Running this request as written returns `400`: Postman cannot mint a valid signature, only the Stripe CLI (`stripe trigger ...`) or a real event can.

### Status codes are the contract
| Code | When |
| --- | --- |
| `200` | understood and handled, including a duplicate event |
| `400` | bad signature or unparseable body - never retried |
| `500` | a known event failed to process - Stripe retries |

Repeat with the same event `id` to see de-duplication: the second call returns `duplicate: true` and changes nothing.

item.name: Stripe webhook: plan catalog sync (provider callback)

request.description:
The same endpoint again - Stripe is the one place plan pricing and limits are meant to be edited going forward, not a Django admin form. Set `metadata.data` (a JSON string) on a Price - or a Product, before it has a price - to this shape, and `product.created/updated` or `price.created/updated` upserts the matching `Plan` row from it.

**Calling fields**, read from the same payload: `has_calls` is one permission for audio and video together, not two - it defaults to `true` (matching the column's own default) when a product's metadata has never mentioned calling at all, so editing a price for an unrelated reason cannot silently switch calling off for a plan nobody has touched calling on. `max_call_participants`, `has_call_recording` and `call_recording_retention_days` are read the same way. `has_screen_share` is never read from metadata - it always just equals `has_calls`, the same rule the Enterprise Plan Builder uses (see `10. Enterprise`).

Matched to a `Plan` by `code` for a `product.created` with no price yet, and by `stripe_product_id` afterwards - a second `price.updated` for the SAME product updates that plan in place rather than creating another one. Running this as written returns `400` for the same signature reason as *Stripe webhook (provider callback)*.

The application server key a browser subscribes with.

Served rather than configured into the web app: the frontend is a static export, so a build-time value could not be rotated without a rebuild and would sit in every cached bundle. The private half never leaves the server.

`enabled` is false when no key pair is configured, so a client can say so instead of offering a switch that does nothing.

Remember this browser, so it can be notified when the app is closed. Send exactly what `subscription.toJSON()` gives you.

**Keyed on the endpoint, not on the account.** The same browser signing in as somebody else MOVES the row to that account - otherwise a shared laptop shows one person's messages, with the sender and the words, to whoever sits down next.

One row per browser: a laptop and a phone both get notified, because a notification that arrived on only one of them looks like it worked.

Turn notifications off for this browser. The web app also calls this on sign-out.

Scoped to your own rows, so an endpoint somebody else registered cannot be removed by guessing it - an endpoint is a URL, and URLs get pasted into places. Silent when there is nothing to delete: "they were already off" is not an error anybody can act on.

A browser that has been wiped needs no call at all - the push service answers 404 or 410 and the row is deleted at the first refusal.

Everything the Plan Builder needs to price a configuration client-side: the base fee, each limit tier (`max_groups`, `max_members_per_group`, `max_admins_per_group`, `storage_gb`), the six toggleable features - including `calls` (one price for audio and video together, matching `billing.Plan.has_calls` being a single flag) and `call_recording` - the analytics tiers, the Communication Credit packages, and the billing intervals with their period discounts.

Public, so the builder can quote a price before anyone signs up. Everything here is database-driven (`PricingCatalogVersion`) - a price change is a new catalog version, never an edit to a live one, so a plan someone already checked out never moves under them.

Prices `configuration` against the active catalog and upserts a draft. Omit `draft_id` to create one (returned as `data.draft_id`, format `ent_draft_<12 hex chars>`); include it to update that same draft again.

**Anonymous-allowed.** Called with no `Authorization` header, the draft is owned by the caller's session instead of an account - only that session (or, once *Attach a draft* is called, that account) can read it back. Called signed in, as this request is when it runs after *Login* earlier in this collection, the account is attached immediately - no separate attach step needed.

`features` now has six keys, all required: the four content ones plus `calls` and `call_recording` - calling, for a custom plan, is priced and bought exactly like any other feature here, unlike the four platform plans (*List plans*), which ship with it on by default. `calls` covers audio AND video together - one price, matching `billing.Plan.has_calls` being a single flag rather than two.

Every value in `limits`, `features` and `credits` is checked against the catalog's active options - an unknown or retired selection is rejected with a `400` and field errors under `data`, never silently clamped to the nearest valid one. The returned `pricing` block is always computed server-side; nothing about price is ever taken from this request body.

Owner-scoped read of one draft - by account if signed in, by the anonymous session that created it otherwise. The `draft_id` alone is never enough: a guessed or shared id from someone else's session returns `404`, the same "not yours looks like it doesn't exist" rule the rest of this API uses.

item.name: Attach a draft to my account

request.description:
Links an anonymous draft to the now-signed-in caller's account - the step a client calls right after login/signup when it already has a `draft_id` from configuring the plan while logged out. Leaves `status` as `"draft"`.

Since *Save a plan configuration draft* above already ran signed in, this draft is already attached to this account - calling it again here is idempotent and just confirms that. Attaching a draft already linked to a **different** account returns `403`.

Revalidates the draft against the **current** active catalog (it may have changed since it was saved), freezes the result into a new `EnterpriseContract` (`contract_number`, e.g. `ENT-2026-000042`), and opens a Stripe Checkout Session for it - one line item per priced selection (base fee first), plus a coupon for the interval discount.

`success_url`/`cancel_url` are required, same as *Subscribe to a plan* in `8. Billing` - Stripe redirects the browser there when the customer finishes or abandons Checkout, and both are checked against `BILLING_ALLOWED_REDIRECT_ORIGINS` (a `400` names the field if the origin isn't trusted).

Returns both the `invoice` breakdown (for a confirmation modal) and `checkout_url` - nothing is charged until the customer completes Checkout, so showing the invoice first and redirecting only on explicit confirmation is safe.

If a selection is no longer active in the catalog at all (not just repriced), this returns `409` with a message safe to show inline, asking the caller to reconfigure and save again rather than silently billing whatever still happens to validate.

The caller's current Enterprise contract, if they have one: `contract_number`, `billing_interval`, `status` (`pending` -> `active` -> `past_due`/`canceled`), the frozen `pricing` snapshot (including its `line_items`), and the underlying Stripe subscription status. `data.contract` is `null` if the caller has never checked out an Enterprise plan.

Same idea as *Billing summary* in `8. Billing`, but for a catalog-driven Enterprise contract instead of a single Plan code.

Current message-credit balance (`data.balance`) plus the paginated ledger behind it (`data.ledger.results`): one row per `allocation` (checkout, or a renewal replenishing the period - no rollover, the balance is replaced, not added to), `usage`, `adjustment`, `expiration` or `refund`.

`data.contract`-less callers (no Enterprise contract yet) get a zero balance and an empty ledger rather than a `404` - there is nothing wrong with the request, there is just nothing to show yet.

item.name: Stripe webhook: enterprise checkout completed (provider callback)

request.description:
**Called by Stripe, not by a client** - the exact same endpoint as *Stripe webhook (provider callback)* in `8. Billing`, not a separate route. Included so the Enterprise shape of `checkout.session.completed` is documented alongside the Plan/credits one: `metadata.kind = "enterprise_contract"` and `metadata.contract_id` are what route this event to Enterprise's own activation logic (mark the contract active, create its entitlements from the frozen configuration snapshot, and write the initial credit-ledger allocation) instead of the Plan-subscription sync.

Same signature verification, status-code contract and de-duplication (by event `id`) as the Billing webhook - running this as written returns `400`, since Postman cannot mint a valid `Stripe-Signature`. Only a real event or `stripe trigger ...` can.

Start an audio or video call in a conversation you are an active member of, **and join it**. The caller is in the call from this response on.

`call_type` is `audio` (the default) or `video`.

### The response
`data.call` is the call. `data.livekit` is what the browser needs to connect to LiveKit **directly**: `url` (the `wss://` address), `token` and `expires_at`. Media never passes through Django. The token is a short-lived JWT for this one room and this one person - it cannot be used to join anything else, or to record or end a call. `LIVEKIT_API_SECRET` stays on the server; only tokens signed with it are ever returned.

What the token lets you *publish* is decided here, not by the client: microphone always, camera only on a `video` call, screen share only if the group owner's plan has it.

### Who may
Active members only. Somebody outside the conversation gets `404` - the same answer as a conversation that does not exist. In a **broadcast** group only admins may start a call. In a one-to-one conversation where either person blocked the other, `403`.

### One live call per conversation
A second start while one is ringing or active returns `409`, with `data.call_id` naming the call to **join** instead.

### Realtime
Everyone else in the conversation is told over the existing websocket (`/ws/chat/`) with a `call.incoming` frame. See the collection description for every frame.

| Status | When |
| --- | --- |
| `201` | started |
| `403` | broadcast group and you are not an admin; blocked |
| `404` | not a member of that conversation |
| `409` | there is already a live call here |
| `429` | 60 starts an hour |
| `503` | LiveKit is not configured or not reachable |

Calls in conversations you are an active member of, newest first, paginated.

Filters: `conversation=<id>` and `status=ringing|active|ended`. `?conversation=<id>&status=active` is how a client finds out whether there is a call to offer to join when it opens a thread.

Ended calls are the call history: who took part, when they joined and left, and for how long.

One call. `participants` holds every stay, not only who is in right now - a client shows the ones whose `left_at` is `null`, and `participant_count` is that number. `duration` is in seconds.

`is_recording` is `true` while a recording is in progress, so a client can show that everyone is being recorded.

No token is ever in here. Somebody who is not in the conversation gets `404` and cannot tell whether the call exists.

Join a live call. Returns the call and a LiveKit token, exactly as *Start a call* does.

Joining moves a ringing call to `active` and tells everyone (`call.accepted`).

**Idempotent.** Joining while already in the call takes no second place and hands back a fresh token - that is what a page refresh needs, and it does not announce an arrival a second time.

### The participant limit
The plan's `max_call_participants` is enforced here, on the server, counted under a lock so two people cannot both take the last place. It is the **group owner's** plan (for a one-to-one call, the person who started it), the same rule as members per group. Nothing in the request can raise it. Somebody already in the call is never turned away for it.

| Status | When |
| --- | --- |
| `200` | in, with a token |
| `403` | the call is full for this plan |
| `404` | not a member of the conversation |
| `409` | the call has ended |
| `429` | 300 joins an hour |

Turn down a call that is ringing. Tells everyone (`call.rejected`).

In a **group**, this only says "not me" - the call carries on. In a **one-to-one** conversation there is nobody else, so declining ends the call (`end_reason: declined`).

You cannot decline your own call (`400`) or one you are already in (`400`). Run this as somebody other than the caller to see it succeed.

Start recording the call. LiveKit's egress service writes the file straight to S3; Django keeps the metadata.

**Who:** whoever started the call, or a group admin. **Plan:** the group owner's plan must include call recording (`has_call_recording` on *List plans*) - Free does not.

Everyone on the call is told (`call.recording.started`) and `call.is_recording` becomes `true`. Only one recording can be in progress per call.

`data.status` is `recording`. The bucket and key are never in an API response.

| Status | When |
| --- | --- |
| `201` | recording |
| `403` | not the starter or an admin, or the plan has no recording |
| `404` | not a member |
| `409` | the call ended, already being recorded, or nobody has connected yet |
| `429` | 30 starts an hour |
| `503` | recording is not configured, or LiveKit is not reachable |

Stop the recording in progress. Same standing as starting it.

Returns at once with `status: stopping`; the file is finalised and uploaded in the background, and LiveKit reports back by webhook, moving it to `completed` (with `size_bytes`, `duration_seconds` and, if the plan has a retention period, `expires_at`).

Ending the call has the same effect - a recording is finished by LiveKit when its room closes.

`400` when nothing is being recorded.

Metadata for every recording of the call, newest first. No download links here - fetch one recording for that.

**Who can see them:** an active member who started the call, administers the group, or was on the call. A member who was never there gets `404`: a recording holds every participant's voice.

One recording's metadata, and - once `status` is `completed` - a `download_url`.

The link is signed for this request and expires in minutes (`LIVEKIT_RECORDING_URL_TTL_SECONDS`, default 300); ask again rather than storing it. It is `null` until the file is ready and after it is deleted.

Same visibility as *List a call's recordings*: `404` for anybody who may not see it.

Delete the recording's file. Whoever started the call, or a group admin.

Returns `204`. The **record stays** (`status: deleted`, with who and when) so a call still says it was recorded; the pointer to the file goes with the file. If S3 cannot delete it, nothing is marked and the request answers `503` - try again.

`409` while the recording is still in progress: stop it first. Recordings past their plan's retention period are deleted automatically each day.

Take yourself out of the call. Records when you left and for how long. **The last person out ends the call** (`end_reason: empty`, or `unanswered` if nobody ever picked up).

Leaving a call you are not in is not an error.

A client that just closes the tab never calls this. LiveKit reports the disconnect by webhook and the place is given back then; a call nobody ended is closed by a sweep.

End the call **for everyone** and close its LiveKit room, which disconnects anybody still in it. Tells the conversation (`call.ended`).

**Who:** whoever started the call, or a group admin (either person, in a one-to-one). Anybody else gets `403`.

Ending a call that has already ended is not an error - in this collection the previous request was the last person leaving, so this returns the ended call as it is.

How LiveKit tells Django what happened in a room - a participant arriving or dropping out, a room closing, a recording finishing. Django cannot see a connection, so this is what frees the place of somebody whose laptop closed, and what completes a recording.

Authenticated by a signature, not a token: the `Authorization` header is a JWT LiveKit makes with the API key and secret, carrying a hash of the body. Configure LiveKit's `webhook:` block with this URL and the same key. Running this request as written returns `400` - Postman cannot mint that signature.

| Status | When |
| --- | --- |
| `200` | verified and handled, including events we ignore |
| `400` | missing or bad signature, or the body was changed |
| `500` | a verified event failed to process - LiveKit retries |

item.name: 12. WhatsApp
item.description:
WhatsApp over each group owner's **own** WhatsApp Business number, connected through Meta's Embedded Signup. The group stays a Loopd'n group - WhatsApp is one more channel into it, like SMS and email, and never a native WhatsApp group.

**Optional.** Nothing happens at signup or login. The two entrances are *profile settings* (Connect WhatsApp Business) and a group's *Invite by WhatsApp*.

Run top to bottom: connect, set templates, attach to `conversation_id`, invite, opt in. The two webhook requests are what Meta sends; the last two requests undo the setup.

request.description:
What the browser needs to start Meta's **Embedded Signup**: `app_id`, `config_id` and `graph_version` for `FB.init` / `FB.login`. All public by design. `enabled` is false when the server has no Meta app configured - hide the connect button then.

**Connecting WhatsApp is optional and never part of signup or login.** The web app offers it from *profile settings* and from a group's *Invite by WhatsApp*.

The WhatsApp Business numbers **you** connected. Paginated. An empty `results` is the cue to show *Connect WhatsApp Business* in profile settings.

Each carries its status (`active`, `error`, `suspended`), the display number and verified name Meta reports, quality rating, template names, and the groups it carries with their `#keyword`. **The business token is never returned** - it is stored encrypted and only ever sent to Meta.

Stores the first connection's id in `whatsapp_connection_id`.

Finish Embedded Signup. In the browser, `FB.login` with `config_id` returns a `code`, and the session-info `message` event carries `waba_id` and `phone_number_id`. Send all three here.

The server then:
1. exchanges `code` for the business's token (needs our app secret, so never done in the browser);
2. asks Meta which WABAs that token covers and **refuses a `waba_id` it does not cover** - the ids from the browser are claims, the token is proof;
3. checks `phone_number_id` belongs to that WABA;
4. subscribes our app to the WABA's webhooks, registers the number for Cloud API, reads its name;
5. stores it with the token encrypted.

Reconnecting a number you already own updates it in place. Stores `whatsapp_connection_id`.

| Status | When |
| --- | --- |
| `201` | connected |
| `400` | `data.reason` is `waba_not_granted`, `number_not_in_waba`, `number_in_use` (another account owns it) or `suspended` |
| `429` | 20 an hour |
| `503` | Meta refused or is unreachable, or WhatsApp is not configured on this server |
One of your connections. Anybody else's is `404`.

The approved templates this number uses. Only these three fields are writable.

WhatsApp allows free-form text only within **24 hours** of the recipient's last message to the business. Outside that window only an approved template may be sent, so each connection needs, approved **on its own WABA**:

- `notification_template_name` - a group message. Body parameters `{{1}}` group, `{{2}}` sender, `{{3}}` text. Category UTILITY.
- `invitation_template_name` - the opt-in request. `{{1}}` inviter, `{{2}}` group, and a quick-reply button whose payload is `START`.

Blank falls back to the server's `WHATSAPP_DEFAULT_TEMPLATE_NAME` / `WHATSAPP_INVITE_TEMPLATE_NAME`. Without a template, recipients outside the window are skipped with a logged reason, never dropped silently.
Re-read the display number, verified name, quality rating and messaging limit from Meta. A revoked token or deregistered number moves the connection to `error`, and the owner must reconnect.

Carry this group over one of **your** connected numbers. Group admins only, and only with a number you own. One number can carry many groups; each gets a `#keyword`, unique on that number, which members in several of its groups use to say which one they mean. Omit `keyword` to derive one from the group name.

Also the way to change the keyword or the two switches: `delivery_enabled` (group messages go out on WhatsApp) and `replies_enabled` (WhatsApp messages are posted into the group). Pointing a group at a different number of yours moves it.

### `data.reason`
A refusal that the web app should act on carries a stable code in `data.reason`:

| reason | meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `whatsapp_not_connected` | the caller has no connected number - **run Embedded Signup**, then retry |
| `choose_connection` | the caller has several numbers - pass `connection` |
| `not_admin` / `not_owner` | only a group admin, with their own number |
| `no_verified_number` | the person has no verified phone to reach |
| `keyword_taken` | another group on that number uses the keyword |
| `not_attached` | this group is not on WhatsApp |

The **Invite by WhatsApp** entrance. Adds the person to the group by phone number (the same permission and block checks as inviting by SMS, but no SMS is sent) and sends the connection's **invitation template**.

If the group is not on WhatsApp yet and you have exactly one connected number, it is attached first. With none, the answer is `400` with `data.reason = "whatsapp_not_connected"` - open Embedded Signup, then retry. With several, pass `connection`.

Their consent starts `pending`: **nothing from the group reaches them until they tap the button or reply START.** An admin typing a number is not that person agreeing, and Meta's policy says the same.

`data.outcome`: `invited`, `not_sent` (see `data.reason`, e.g. no invitation template), `already_opted_in`, or `declined` - somebody who opted out is **not asked again**; only they can undo it, by sending START.

### `data.reason`
A refusal that the web app should act on carries a stable code in `data.reason`:

| reason | meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `whatsapp_not_connected` | the caller has no connected number - **run Embedded Signup**, then retry |
| `choose_connection` | the caller has several numbers - pass `connection` |
| `not_admin` / `not_owner` | only a group admin, with their own number |
| `no_verified_number` | the person has no verified phone to reach |
| `keyword_taken` | another group on that number uses the keyword |
| `not_attached` | this group is not on WhatsApp |

| Status | When |
| --- | --- |
| `201` | handled - read `data.outcome` |
| `400` | see `data.reason` above; or a phone number without a `display_name` |
| `429` | 60 invitations an hour |

Ask somebody **already in the group** to receive it on WhatsApp too. Admins only. Pass `participant` (their membership id) instead of a phone number. They are reached at their **verified** phone number and nowhere else; with none, `400 no_verified_number`.

item.name: My WhatsApp opt-in for a group

request.description:
The caller's own answer, from inside the app: `enabled: true` opts in (a recorded, explicit opt-in - it may also undo a STOP, because the member is the one choosing), `false` declines this group. Nobody can opt anybody else in.

`400 not_attached` when the group is not on WhatsApp; `400 no_verified_number` until the caller verifies a phone.

**Called by Meta, not the app.** The handshake Meta performs when the callback URL is saved in the app dashboard: it answers with `hub.challenge` as plain text when `hub.verify_token` equals `WHATSAPP_WEBHOOK_VERIFY_TOKEN`, and `403` otherwise.

**Called by Meta, not the app.** One webhook for every connected number; `metadata.phone_number_id` says which connection. Signed with `X-Hub-Signature-256` (HMAC-SHA256 of the body with the app secret) - unsigned requests are `401` whenever `WHATSAPP_APP_SECRET` is set, so this example only works against a server without one.

What a message does:
- `STOP` / `START` opt out of / back into **every group on that business number**. `HELP` and `GROUPS` list the group tags.
- Anything else is routed to one group: `#keyword text` names it; a swipe-reply goes to the quoted message's group; one group on the number means that one; otherwise the group they last talked in or heard from. Still ambiguous: they are asked, and nothing is posted.
- It is posted only for an **opted-in** active member, with `source: "whatsapp"`, and then reaches the app, SMS, email and other WhatsApp members as any message does.
- Strangers get silence. Media is not posted yet; members are told so.

Items are de-duplicated one by one, so Meta's retries never post twice. `500` means "retry", and only for an item that failed unexpectedly.

**Called by Meta, not the app.** A message we sent moved on: `sent`, `delivered`, `read` or `failed`. Updates the delivery log, and never backwards - a late `sent` after `read` leaves it `read`. `pricing.category` is kept so an owner can see what Meta billed them for.

The other fields handled: `account_update` with `PARTNER_REMOVED` (the owner removed our app in Business Manager) disconnects the number and detaches its groups; `phone_number_quality_update` refreshes the messaging limit.
Stop carrying this group over WhatsApp. A group admin, or the owner of the number, may do it. The number stays connected and keeps serving its other groups.

Disconnect the number: our app is unsubscribed from the WABA, the stored token is erased, and **every group it carried is detached at once**. Nothing more is sent from it or accepted on it. Connect again through Embedded Signup to undo.

Delete a group. **Admins only, and it releases the phone number.**

Returns `204`. A plain member gets `403`; somebody who is not in the group gets `404` and is not told it exists. One-to-one conversations cannot be deleted - they belong to two people equally and neither can end it for both.
